title: Social and behavioral consequences of alcohol consumption and expectancy: A meta-analysis

claims.statement: In laboratory experiments that told people they were drinking alcohol or not, and separately gave them alcohol or not, believing they had drunk alcohol increased how much men drank in a short taste test and went with greater sexual arousal, while the alcohol actually drunk, at the low doses these designs allow, affected memory, physical sensations, mood and coordination but not detectably how much people drank; these experiments say little about higher doses or drinking outside the laboratory. In one such experiment in Madison, Wisconsin (published 1973), 64 men, 32 with a history of alcohol problems who were still drinking (treatment admissions, repeated drunkenness arrests, or past membership of Alcoholics Anonymous or a rehabilitation programme; the study's 'alcoholic' group) and 32 social drinkers, were randomly assigned within each group to be told that their drinks were vodka and tonic or tonic only, and to be given one or the other; men told vodka drank about twice as much in a 15-minute taste test as men told tonic (about 18.8 against 9.1 fluid ounces, from the table; the text prints 17.77 for the first; d about 1.1, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.6, editors' calculation), whatever was in the glass and in both groups, while receiving vodka made no detectable difference (13.2 against 14.7 ounces when given tonic; difference −1.5 ounces, 95% CI −5.8 to +2.8, editors' calculation, so a moderate effect cannot be ruled out). Drinking was mostly highest in the first 3 minutes and then fell, with no sign of drinking getting out of control; blood alcohol at the end, estimated rather than measured, averaged 0.031% to 0.093%; there were 8 men per condition; and the men with alcohol problems were older (mean age 46.75 against 37.19 years) (Marlatt et al., 1973). A 1986 meta-analysis of 36 such experiments published before September 1985 found significant pooled effects of believing one had drunk alcohol on sexual arousal (mean g 0.31, 9 studies) and on drinking or wanting to drink (0.52, 3 studies, all in the same direction, this experiment included), none on memory-related information processing, mood, physical sensations, motor performance or bodily arousal, and a non-significant effect in the opposite direction on aggression (−0.13); the alcohol itself impaired information processing (0.53, 5 studies) and motor performance (0.64, 3 studies), changed physical sensations (0.64) and improved mood (0.21), and did not detectably change drinking (−0.04) or sexual arousal (−0.02). The sizes from that analysis are rough: about 35% to 45% of effects of unknown size were set to zero, studies were not weighted, no confidence intervals were given, and doses and participants were not extracted; and in 18 of 20 experiments that did not first ask participants which drink they had received, the alcohol itself changed what they believed they had drunk, so the design seldom separates alcohol from belief (Hull & Bond, 1986). Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Marlatt et al. (1973), fluid ounces drunk in 15 minutes: told vodka about 18.8 (Table 1; 17.77 in the text) vs told tonic 9.12, F = 20.59, df 1/56, p < .01, d about 1.13 (95% CI 0.63 to 1.64; editors' calculation); given vodka 13.19 vs given tonic 14.69, F = .50, difference −1.5 oz (95% CI −5.8 to +2.8; editors' calculation); cell means, men with alcohol problems told tonic 10.94 and 10.25, told vodka 23.87 and 22.13; social drinkers 9.31 and 5.94, 14.62 and 14.44; estimated end-of-task blood alcohol .031% to .093%. Hull & Bond (1986), mean g (unweighted; effects of unknown size set to zero; no intervals), expectancy vs alcohol: sexual arousal 0.306 (Z = 2.861) vs −0.017; drinking or desire to drink 0.523 (Z = 2.870; study values 0.66, 0.52, 0.39) vs −0.040; aggression −0.131 vs 0.255 (p < .10); information processing −0.002 vs 0.5344; physical sensations 0.0450 vs 0.6440; motor performance 0.1230 vs 0.6360; mood 0.061 vs 0.209; bodily arousal 0.046 vs −0.225 (not significant). For Marlatt et al. the meta-analysis averages amount drunk with sip counts (0.66), which understates the effect on amount (about 1.1).
